claims.claim: Return to air-water/air-glass interface experiment.
Now investigate optically denser-to-less-dense direction.
Semicylindrical glass experiment: move emitter to lower half of disk.
Send incident ray along earlier refracted radius.
Light exits glass along earlier incident-ray route: incident/refracted routes reverse.
Inside glass there is reflected ray besides incident ray; frosted surface makes reflected trace visible; figure156.
Reflection angle equals incidence angle.
n denotes glass relative to air, n>1; air relative to glass is1/n.
Glass is first medium, air second; inverted relative-index law follows.
Equation6.12: sin(alpha)/sin(beta)=1/n.
Move emitter to increase incidence; reflected angle (equal to incidence) and refraction angle also increase.
Refraction angle larger than incidence in oblique transmitting case.
Rearrange6.12 to sin(beta)=n sin(alpha); n>1 implies strict sine/angle inequality in its applicable domain.
Entering optically less dense medium bends away from interface normal.
Observed reflected brightness/energy increases and refracted brightness/energy decreases as incidence increases.
Transmitted beam energy weakens particularly rapidly as beta approaches90degrees.
Nearly interface-parallel refracted beam shown in157; reflected energy approaches100percent.
Alpha0 corresponds to maximum refracted angle beta90degrees.
For alpha>alpha0, refracted beam disappears and all light reflects: total reflection.
Original states alpha>=alpha0 at dense/less-dense interface; equality requires modern boundary distinction, not source-snapshot editing.
Alpha0 corresponding to beta90degrees defines critical angle.
At sin(beta)=1,6.12 gives sin(alpha0)=1/n, equation6.13.
Original approximate water critical angle48degrees35minutes, with displayed n1.33.
Original approximate glass critical angle41degrees50minutes, with displayed n1.5.
Original approximate diamond critical angle24degrees40minutes, with displayed n2.4.
Air is second medium in all three numeric examples.
Figure158 rays originate from a source a little below water surface.
Stronger light is represented by thicker drawn rays.
Fill glass with water and raise it slightly above eye level.
Look from below through glass wall at water surface; total reflection makes surface look bright/silvery.
Fiber optics uses total reflection to transmit light and images through transparent flexible fibers: light guides.
Cylindrical glass fibers have transparent coating with smaller refractive index.
Repeated total reflection allows propagation along straight or curved paths; original says any path, requiring bend/domain qualification.
Many fibers gathered into bundle/braid; each fiber carries an image element; figure159.
Fiber bundles can examine internal organs in medicine.
Placing an ordinary lamp inside would cause unwanted heating, motivating guided illumination.

originalMathematicalRequirements: Alpha/beta measured to normal; n remains dense material relative to air, n>1, not redefined as air/material after reversal.
6.12 unchanged sine ratio1/n, with nonzero ratio domain and separate normal-incidence zero case.
sin(beta)=n sin(alpha) unchanged; strict beta>alpha only for positive incidence with a real transmitting ray up to critical boundary.
6.13 sin(alpha0)=1/n; generalized critical sine is n_less/n_dense in ordinary transparent media, requiring n_dense>n_less.

At critical equality beta90degrees is the grazing boundary. For alpha>alpha0 Snell would require sine>1; no propagating refracted ray. Do not describe supercritical refraction as an ordinary90degree ray.

Original three rounded n and approximate degree/minute values must not be asserted as three exact numerical equalities. Modern explanation/computed approximations must be explicit, source values/snapshots unchanged.
modernSCIDemands: Keep dense-to-less-dense direction, reversibility and experimental emitter/radius/frosted-surface information.

Any reflected/transmitted intensity trend needs ordinary lossless-interface, fixed incident beam and polarization applicability; source observation is not a universal statement for every polarization.

Explain equality at critical as limiting grazing boundary separately from alpha>alpha0 full internal reflection; no greater-than-one sine, finite normal transmitted flux at grazing, or fabricated physical ray above critical.
Do not silently change quoted oldbook alpha>=alpha0 inside source snapshot; mark modern clarification as not source quote/erratum.
Fiber cladding index must remain smaller than core index; propagation follows TIR incidence conditions, not arbitrary tight bends with no loss.
Image transport by bundles needs retained relative fiber arrangement/coherent image correspondence; each single fiber carries an element, not an entire automatic image.
Medical illumination/internal-organ observation and original unwanted lamp-heating information must remain, without adding clinical efficacy/safety claims.
Preserve four figure identities/refs/captions and thick-ray convention; no figure-derived scientific conclusions guessed from unresolved pixels.
